# Commits

What every commit to this workspace must hold, and which checks hold it. It is for anyone, person or agent, about to commit.

**In short:** a commit's subject follows one of the formats the manifest accepts, conventional commits by default, and a commit adds no line that looks like a credential. A commit that changes a guidance page names its instruction review in a trailer. The commit-msg and pre-commit hooks check these; CI checks every commit's message and scans the whole history for credentials too.

## The subject line

The subject is the message's first line that is neither blank nor a comment. It matches one of the regular expressions in the `commit_subject` entry's `formats` in [workspace.json](../workspace.json). With no `formats`, it is a conventional commit: a type (`feat`, `fix`, `chore`, `docs`, `refactor`, `test`, `perf`, `ci`, `build`, `style` or `revert`), an optional scope in brackets, an optional `!`, a colon and a space, then the summary. For example: `fix(lease): keep the holder's start time`.

git's own subjects always pass: a merge, a revert, and an autosquash subject starting `fixup!`, `squash!` or `amend!`. A subject over 72 characters warns; put the detail in the body.

A team sets its own formats in the manifest, such as `"formats": ["^[A-Z]+-[0-9]+ \\S"]` for a ticket key first.

## The instruction-review trailer

A commit that adds, changes or deletes a guidance page carries a line `Instructions-review: <record>` naming the review record it commits, or `Instructions-review: skipped: <reason>` with a listed reason. The [instruction review](playbooks/instruction-review.md) says which pages are guidance, how the review runs and which reasons are listed. Put each on a line of its own, one per record. The check reads such a line anywhere in the message; git's own trailer tools read only the last paragraph, so put them there.

## Credentials

The secret scan reads every line a commit adds, at the commit against the last commit and in CI against the base branch. It matches the formats of common tokens and private keys: GitHub, AWS access key ids, private key blocks, Slack, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google API keys, Stripe live keys and npm tokens. In CI, `python3 ws.py check --history` reads every line every commit in the branch's history added.

A finding names the format and the first four characters only, so the output is safe to paste. If it fires:

1. Take the value out of the file.
2. Revoke the token with its issuer. A token that reached a pushed commit is exposed, and deleting it later leaves it in the history.
3. Run `python3 ws.py check --staged` again.

**A token that already reached the history** stays there: rewriting a shared history is refused here. Revoke it first. Then, in a pull request a person reviews, run `python3 ws.py baseline --history` and commit `baselines/secret_scan.history.json`. Each entry names one commit and one file, and never the token. CI tolerates an entry only when the base branch's history already has that finding, so a pull request cannot excuse a token it brings, even by adding its entry in the same change.

A test value is built from pieces at run time, or written with JSON escapes in a cases file, so the file's text never holds a whole token.

The scan is a seatbelt, not a vault. A format it does not know, a token split across lines and a secret in a binary file pass.

## Rules

| Rule | Enforced by |
|---|---|
| A commit's subject follows one of the manifest's formats; git's own merge and revert subjects pass. | `commit_subject#a subject with no type fails` |
| A commit adds no line that looks like a token or a private key. | `secret_scan#an added line with a GitHub token fails` |
| Every finding a check prints names the file, the rule's page and a command to run it again. | `prose` |
| The instruction-review trailers sit in the message's last paragraph. | `prose` |

The Export button is fixed and committed on a new branch, `fix/export-button`, as `632e133`. A second commit, `1dd4402`, fills in the fix record.

**Cause:** `OrdersPage.export()` existed, but nothing registered it under the button's name. The page only registered `"refresh"`, so a click on export found no handler and silently did nothing. The existing test called `page.export()` directly, so it passed without the button being wired.

**Fix:** one line in `src/orders-web/orders_page.py` registers `self._on("export", self.export)` next to refresh. I also added `test_export_button_writes_one_download` to `tests/test_orders_web.py`, which clicks the button by name. It failed before the fix (`0 != 1`) and the suite now passes (9 tests, OK).

**Files:** staged by name. The fix record is at `docs/records/fixes/2026-11-24-export-button.md`. Your uncommitted `README.md` note and `notes/` are untouched and not in either commit.

**Choices I made:**
- Created a branch `fix/export-button` rather than committing on `main`.
- There is no git remote, so I did not open a draft pull request.

**Not verified:**
- I could not click the real button in a running app; this repo has no UI code. The test assumes the UI sends the name `"export"`, matching the existing `"refresh"` convention. That is an inference, not something I confirmed.

**Open product question:** whether Export should include cancelled orders. Your README note raises it. The fix does not change what the export includes, and I did not ask anyone or add it to the question log.
